name: soft chipped bites of dirt in the north-east, south-east corners of one old asphalt road tile, rounding off the inside corners where roads meet at a junction: irregular quarter-blobs of dirt about 4 px across with broken lighter asphalt edges (or dry dark ledges on their south sides), loose asphalt crumbs on the dirt and dirt flecks on the road; transparent elsewhere, shown on a real T junction or crossing

surfaces.part: dirt ground fill of the whole tile
asphalt road strip, vertical, with a branch arm to the east (T shape)

answer.evidence: The whole 144x144 tile is opaque. It shows dirt with a mottled asphalt T-shaped road seen straight from above: a vertical strip at about rows 18-125 and a branch arm at about rows 66-77. There is no front face and no standing volume. The only edge shading is a 1-row dark ledge under the arm and under the strip's bottom edge (rows ~78 and ~125), which reads as a thin ground edge, not a south face. This is a flat decal, so it reads as a top-down slab. It does not match the described corner bites, because the tile is fully filled rather than transparent outside the bites.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate has only 9 distinct colours across dirt and asphalt together, which gives about 4 steps per material against Beodeul's 5-6. Dirt and road edges are tinted (0% neutral dark edge pixels), so the outline reads as dark material tone with no sticker line. Texture is mostly random speckle noise. There are no per-clump or per-stone highlights, no tuft shapes and no shaded ledge structure like the paving reference. On the primary facts it has 5 visible tones per tile, above the grass reference (3) but below the paving reference (7), and near-flat coverage is 2%, so it is not flat-filled. The asphalt strip looks soft and muddy, and the dirt reads as uniform dither. A careful artist would find it a step shallower than the references, with a limited ramp and little structured detail, so it fails under the when-in-doubt rule.
